sections.html:
Just north of Boston, Medford is a Middlesex County city that the Mystic River crosses from west to southeast. It covers 8.66 square miles. The 2020 census counted 59,659 residents in 24,413 households and 25,770 housing units, with 5.3 percent vacant.

Part of the 2,060 acre Middlesex Fells Reservation lies in the north, shared with Winchester, Stoneham, Melrose and Malden. Tufts University has its campus along the Medford and Somerville line, mostly on Medford Hillside, and a steady student and staff population keeps the rental market active in nearby streets, which is worth knowing if you own a multi-family house on or near Medford Hillside. Landlords there often field offers from buyers who plan to keep renting the units.

People in Medford usually name their neighborhood first, and each has its own feel.

  • West Medford, described as the most affluent area, with a historic African American neighborhood dating to the Civil War.
  • South Medford, traditionally Italian.
  • Wellington, also called East Medford.
  • Fulton Heights, or The Heights, in North Medford.
  • Brooks Estates, Glenwood, Lawrence Estates and Medford Hillside, where Tufts is mostly situated.

For a listing or a private sale, the neighborhood name tells a buyer more about a house than the city name does, so use it.

sections.h2: Why many Medford homes are old
sections.html:
English colonists settled Medford in 1630 as part of Charlestown, and it became a city in 1892. The Boston and Maine Railroad reached Medford Center in 1847, and farmland was divided into house lots starting in the 1840s and 1850s, so many houses date from the 1800s and early 1900s.

Medford made tiles, crackers, bricks, rum and clipper ships, and the first toll bridge over the Mystic went up in 1637 where the Cradock Bridge stands today. Historic sites include the Peter Tufts House at 350 Riverside Avenue, thought to be the oldest all-brick building in New England. Houses in the old Ship Street Historic District around Riverside Avenue are some of the oldest, and an old house can mean old systems.

Medford has both Orange Line and Green Line subway service, plus a commuter rail stop and many bus routes.

ServiceWhere in Medford
Orange LineWellington station, opened in 1975
Green LineMedford/Tufts and Ball Square, opened in 2022 as part of the GLX project
Commuter Rail, Lowell LineWest Medford
MBTA busesRoutes 80, 94, 95, 96, 99, 100, 101, 108 and 134, plus express route 354

Interstate 93 runs north and south through the city, and state routes 16, 28, 38 and 60 cross it. Houses close to the new Green Line stops sit in a part of the city where transit changed recently, which can matter to buyers of all kinds.

sections.h2: Selling a rental or an inherited house
sections.html:
Landlords sometimes decide to sell after repeated turnover, damage or a change in family plans. A cash buyer can take a house with tenants or one left empty, so say which yours is.

If you inherited a house, you may need probate steps before you can sell, depending on how it was held. Speak with a Massachusetts attorney about that first, then share the address and condition with a buyer. Often the sale can go forward as soon as whoever holds authority to sell has it, and a cash buyer will usually wait while that is settled.

Before a Medford sale can close, the fire department must certify your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms.

Owners are told to find the year the house was built and the date of its last building permit, make a list of every alarm with its manufacture date, and replace any that are expired or undated. Battery smoke alarms past 10 years need sealed 10 year photoelectric replacements with a hush feature. Test the new units, then call the fire department, which charges a fee for the inspection and certificate.

The deed excise under Chapter 64D, Section 1 is two dollars for each five hundred dollars of price or fraction of it, outside Barnstable County. Deeds are recorded at a county registry. Medford's county, Middlesex, has a South registry in Cambridge and a North registry in Lowell.

Ask Medford's city offices about permits, open violations and any tax bills before you close. Your contract and attorney will say who pays the excise.

Because a cash buyer is not waiting on a mortgage lender, the closing date can follow your needs.

  1. You give the address, condition, any tenants and your timing.
  2. The buyer looks the house over and sends a written offer.
  3. You accept, and an attorney takes over title work and the purchase and sale agreement.
  4. The alarm certificate and payoff letters are lined up.
  5. The deed is recorded and you receive the proceeds.

Ask any buyer how they reach their number, since an offer should reflect the house itself. Then compare the net result with listing, counting repairs, showings and months of carrying costs.

With no lender there is no bank appraisal, no loan commitment and no financing contingency that can unravel days before closing. Showings shrink to a visit or two, and nobody asks you to repaint, patch the roof or empty every closet first.

State requirements remain. The alarm certificate, title search, payoff letters and deed recording still happen, and your attorney still reviews the contract. What disappears is the lender's schedule, which is where many conventional sales lose weeks.

Gather the newest tax bill, any water balance, a mortgage payoff statement, lease copies and receipts for big repairs. For estate property, add the papers that show who may sign the deed. A complete folder lets a buyer commit to a price and a closing date you can count on, and it saves your attorney from chasing documents in the final week.

Once you accept, the attorney orders a title search that lists mortgages, liens and unpaid charges, and each is paid off or released. The alarm inspection is booked, and the deed is prepared for the registry. At closing you sign the deed and settlement statement, your lenders are paid from the proceeds, and you receive the balance.

With no lender approval to wait on, the usual delays in a Medford sale are an old lien and an alarm check booked too late. Start both the week the contract is signed. Ask for the closing date and the alarm certificate responsibility in writing, and keep copies of every payoff letter. If a tenant lives in the house, tell the buyer when the lease ends so the sale and the move line up.

faqs.q: How many people live in Medford, MA?
faqs.a: The 2020 census counted 59,659 residents in Medford, living in 24,413 households.

faqs.q: Is Medford close to the T?
faqs.a: Yes. Wellington is on the Orange Line, and Medford/Tufts and Ball Square are on the Green Line, which opened in 2022. West Medford has Lowell Line commuter rail.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke and CO certificate to sell in Medford?
faqs.a: Yes. A certificate of compliance from the local fire department is required when you sell or transfer a home. Call the Medford fire department for the fee and scheduling.

faqs.q: What is the deed excise tax when I sell in Medford?
faqs.a: It is two dollars for each five hundred dollars of the sale price or fraction of it. Your contract and attorney will confirm which party pays.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Medford house that I inherited?
faqs.a: Often yes, once whoever holds authority to sell has it, which may require probate. Speak with a Massachusetts attorney about that, then share the address and condition with us.
